1:
Whether the release cancelled the debt or merely suspended the suit is the question the chapter turns on, and Henry sets out both sides before choosing. Many good expositors, he reports, think it forbids only the exacting of the debt during the year of release, since no harvest was gathered then and payment could not be expected, so that the debt was not extinguished but the process stayed; others think it a release for ever, which seems to him the more probable, though under limitations — that the debtor was an Israelite, an alien having no benefit of the law, that he was poor, and that he had borrowed not for trade but for the subsistence of his family. Either way, he holds, a debtor afterwards able to pay was bound in conscience to do so, though the creditor could never again recover it by law.

Gill is exercised by two narrower questions. The release, he insists, was not of servants, since they were not dismissed until they had served six years, and if a sabbatical year freed them they might go out after a month or two; the jubilee released them whenever it fell, the sabbatical year did not. And he presses at the end of hard: not at the latter extremity of the seventh year, for if a poor man's debt might be exacted up to its close it would be no year of rest at all, but at the first extremity of it. Wesley reads the phrase only to fix which year is meant, the last of the seven, identifying it with the sabbatical year. Ellicott places the law historically, as an extension of what stands in Exodus 21 and Leviticus 25: not only a manumission of Hebrew slaves and a sabbath for the land in the seventh year, but a release of debts as well, of which all Israelites must have the benefit. Clarke gives the chapter's argument and refers his reader back to his own notes on those passages.

Why the foreigner was excepted is answered two ways, and the two are not close. Keil takes trouble to defend the rule: the word means a stranger of another nation standing in no inward relation to Israel, distinct from the foreigner who lived among the Israelites and had a claim on their protection and pity; the rule breathes no hatred of foreigners but simply allows the Israelite the right of every creditor to demand his debts, and there was no severity in it, because foreigners could get their ordinary income in the seventh year as in any other. Calvin gives a reason with no such warmth: it was by no means just that despisers of the Law should enjoy the sabbatical benefit, when God had conferred the privilege on his elect people alone.

Calvin alone asks what the law was for and what remains of it. We are not bound by it now, he grants, and it would not even be expedient that it should be in use; but its object ought still to be maintained, that we not be too rigid in exacting our debts, especially from the needy bowed down by poverty. The ancient people's condition was different: one race, one common inheritance, fraternal association to be sustained as if they were one family. From this he draws a political reason. Since God had once enfranchised them, the best plan for preserving their liberty for ever was to maintain a condition of mediocrity, lest a few persons of immense wealth oppress the general body; for the rich, if permitted constantly to increase in wealth, would have tyrannized over the rest, and God put by this law a restraint on immoderate power. He adds that when rest was given to the land it was just that the whole people, for whose sake the sabbath was instituted, should enjoy some relaxation.
4:
The clause rendered save when there shall be no poor among you is read five ways by six commentators, and the differences are grammatical, not merely emphatic. Gill takes it as a genuine exception: where there are no poor the law cannot operate, since it was never designed to screen rich men from paying their just debts but only such as were really poor and unable to pay. He then reports a second reading he does not adopt, that some take the words as a promise, rendering them nevertheless, and that the Targum of Jonathan suggests there would be no poor at all if Israel kept the commandments. Wesley and Ellicott both prefer the marginal rendering, to the end that there be no poor among you, so that the clause states the reason of the law — that none be impoverished and ruined by a rigid exaction of debts — Ellicott adding the alternative to such an extent that, and the caution that those who can well afford to pay need not be excused. Keil parses it as a jussive and so gets an imperative: only let there be no poor with thee. On his reading the sense is that the Israelite need not remit a foreigner's debt but has only to take care that he does not himself cause or increase poverty by oppressing the brethren who have borrowed of him — and Keil notes that so understood the clause is not at variance with the later statement that the poor would never cease out of the land. Clarke settles the same tension in thirteen words by making the promise comparative.

Ellicott alone traces the clause forward. He takes it as the source of the description in the Acts of the Apostles of the first believers, that great grace was upon them all because neither was there among them any that lacked, and repeats the connection at the next verse and the next again, noting that Rashi expounds the passage in the very spirit of it. He also draws the conclusion he wants from it: the blessing promised need not be equal and universal prosperity, provided that those who have the good things of this world will always remember the poor to such an extent that no member of the community is left in want.

On the lending and ruling the two grammarians work the vocabulary. Keil distinguishes the verb's two stems, one meaning to give a pledge in order to borrow and the other to cause a pledge to be given, that is, to lend upon pledge; and he explains the ruling as simply the consequence of superiority in wealth. Ellicott finds the root closely connected with the word for a slave, and quotes the proverb that the borrower is servant to the lender.

Calvin reads the promise as a movement from the particular to the general. Having taught that they might expect from God's blessing much more than they bestowed on the poor, he says, Moses now recalls their attention to the covenant itself, since whatever they have derives from that original fountain of grace, when God made them inheritors of the land — and God, having then promised abundant produce, indicates by that promise that if they were mean and niggardly they would themselves cause the land to be barren. The lending to all nations and the reigning over the Gentiles he takes as amplification rather than prediction, and draws from the whole a conclusion sharper than anyone else's: if there were any in want among them, it would arise from the wickedness and depravity of the people themselves. Gill guards the promise from the other side, that God gives an absolute promise without respect to anything, but a conditional one — as the promises of temporal good things to Israel were — according as the condition is performed.
7:
How the promise that there should be no poor stands with the declaration that the poor shall never cease is answered five ways, and no two are the same. Gill makes it conditional and unfulfilled: had they been obedient they would have been so blessed that there would have been none, as the Targums say, but God foresaw they would not keep his commands and foretold accordingly. Ellicott distinguishes falling into poverty from remaining in it — there will always be men falling in, and it is our business to see they do not remain in want, so the poor never cease except by the provision their brethren make; and he adds flatly that God will never make all men absolutely equal in this world. Keil grounds the permanence in providence, that the poor will never cease even in a land richly blessed, because poverty is not only the penalty of sin but is ordained by God for punishment and discipline. Clarke turns it into a mercy to the giver: God leaves the poor among men to exercise compassion, since without occasions for it a man would soon become a Stoic or a brute. Calvin denies any contradiction at all, since the earlier prohibition meant only that if any were reduced to beggary they should not be cast out and forsaken.

Ellicott states his method openly here, as nowhere else in the chapter: he has borrowed Rashi's comments almost entire, to show how well the Jews have understood the true principles of Christian charity from the law of Moses, that people having always been remarkable for kindness to its own poor. What he passes on is a series of practical rulings — that some men grudge whether they give or not, which is why the heart is forbidden to harden, and some stretch out the hand and yet close it, which is why the hand is forbidden to shut; that if the man will not take it as a gift it should be granted him as a loan; that sufficient for his need does not oblige you to make him rich, though that which he wanteth may extend to a horse to ride on; and that one who has promised receives the reward of the promise as well as of the deed — rulings Gill reports independently under the commentator's other name.

The wicked heart of the ninth verse divides them. Gill takes the Hebrew as a heart of Belial and personifies accordingly: a worthless heart, without a yoke, unsubjected to the law of God, in which Belial, the prince of this world, works effectually. Clarke reads the same phrase as an adjective, a belial heart meaning a good-for-nothing or unprofitable one, and Keil parses it grammatically, worthlessness standing as the predicate, so that what is forbidden is a worthless thought arising in the heart. On the evil eye Clarke is fullest: it signifies a covetous disposition, and our Lord opposes it to the single eye, the man of liberal and benevolent mind, since covetousness darkens the soul while liberality enlightens it. He also hears the cry of the wronged poor as a consolation, that they have a sure friend in God.

On the manner of giving all insist on the disposition rather than the sum. Wesley says the gift must come not only with an open hand but with a cheerful mind, without which a man's charity is uncharitable and not accepted by God. Clarke allows only one measure: benevolence in proportion to the other's distress and to your own ability, and no other rule to regulate charity. Calvin adds a point of timing nobody else notices, that they were to relieve their poor brethren promptly at the beginning of the release year, as if they would have the money back in days — and observes that in forbidding a hardened heart God signifies that avarice is always cruel.
12:
Which seventh year is meant divides them sharply. Keil states it flatly: the year of release here is not the sabbatical year but the seventh year of the man's bondage, and what introduces the law is not the sabbatical provision just given but the poverty which compelled Hebrews to sell themselves. Wesley reckons the same way, computing the six years from the beginning of the servitude. Henry agrees and adds a second release, that if the jubilee fell before the six years were out that would discharge him. Ellicott takes the opposite view and draws the consequence: it is the sabbatical year whenever it came, so that it would rarely happen that a Hebrew slave served the full six years.

How a Hebrew came to be a slave is canvassed by several. Gill reports from Jarchi that a man might be sold by the sanhedrim for theft but a woman might not, though a father might sell an under-age daughter for a handmaid, and a man in poverty sell himself. Keil, explaining why the law is repeated here when it stands already in Exodus 21, holds the repetition was not to extend it to Hebrew women. Henry alone states a principle from it, that God's Israel were a free people and must not be compelled to perpetual slavery, as God's spiritual Israel are called unto liberty.

Ellicott's note on the furnishing is the most remarkable thing in the chapter. Taking from the Jewish commentator that Hebrew slavery was chiefly a consequence of theft, he concludes that under Jewish law even convicted thieves, when their servitude was over, were to be provided with the means of obtaining an honest livelihood — and then turns the observation against his own country, remarking that this state of things is above the attainments of Christian England at the present date. His general point is that those who had fallen into poverty must, their time served, be provided with means for a fresh start.

How liberal the furnishing was to be is itself disputed. Gill presses the Hebrew as far as it will go, rendering it loading thou shalt load him, so the man is given as much as he can carry and well stand up under; and the word carries the sense of chains worn about the neck for ornament, so the dismissal was to be honourable, with plain marks of respect. Calvin sets a ceiling on exactly this: the command to furnish him out of winepress and floor and flock does not mean they were to be enriched or that a large provision should be assigned, but lays a just constraint on the rich, whose abundance supplied the means of liberality. He refuses to treat the law as coercive — it is no civil enactment for extorting from the avaricious more than they will give, the rule being that God loves a cheerful giver — while insisting that since Hebrew slaves were brethren God would not have them placed in a worse condition than hirelings; and he ends by calling the gifts both gratuitous and a just compensation for their labours. Clarke itemises what the three sources yield — cattle to breed with, corn for seed and bread, wine for present necessity — and gives the reason plainly: during his service the man made no property for himself, having been always honest, and now leaves with nothing to begin the world with.

On the motive drawn from Egypt they diverge instructively. Keil observes that this is the standing reason given throughout the law for compassion toward foreigners, servants, widows, orphans and the poor alike. Wesley reads the spoils as wages: God brought them out with riches which, because the Egyptians would not pay, he gave them as a just recompense for their service — and therefore the Israelite is to follow the example and send his servant out furnished.
16:
Why a law of release should provide for refusing release is explained best by Keil, and his reason is humane rather than legal: the provision is repeated from Exodus 21 to guard against an application of the law that would be cruelty rather than love, since manumission is an act of love only where the man set free has some hope of getting a living for himself, and where there is no such prospect compelling him to accept freedom might be equivalent to thrusting him away. He pauses to dismiss a critic in passing, calling the claim that the judicial process required here seems not to have been usual in the author's own time a worthless argument from silence.

Where the ear was bored Gill will not take at face value. Not the door of the master's house, he says, following the Targum of Jonathan, but that of the sanhedrim or court of judicature, before which the man was to be brought to declare his wish to continue with his master. Clarke refers the reader to his earlier note and adds nothing. On the phrase for ever Keil is content with lifelong, while Wesley allows the shorter term as an alternative — all the time of his life, or at least till the year of jubilee.

The maidservant raises a real difficulty, since the earlier law says she shall not go out as the menservants do, and Ellicott takes some trouble over it. The earlier text, he argues, does not say she shall not go out at all but that she shall not go out on the same principle, the exceptions being specified there; the general right of release is what is stated here. From the Jewish commentator he takes one difference, that women were not liable to be sold for theft as men were but might be sold by their parents in infancy, with the consequence that a girl not yet marriageable when the first sabbatical year arrived would obtain her freedom absolutely, the exceptional cases being then impossible; and he concludes that an unmarried female slave's rights were generally the same as a man's. Wesley reads the same clause as covering both branches of the law, that she is either to be dismissed with plenty or engaged to perpetual servitude by the same rites.

What it means that the servant was worth a double hired servant divides them without being settled. Calvin offers two possibilities without deciding: either that the slave's life was more laborious, heavier tasks being required of slaves than of free men who are paid for their work, or that he had completed twice as long a period as hirelings were usually engaged for. Keil names both readings and rejects both — the first because it cannot be proved that a day-labourer generally hired himself out for three years, the second because it reduces the clause to saying that the man worked harder and often by night. Calvin, meanwhile, is more interested in the tone of the verse than its arithmetic, observing that God reproves the Jews' mean and niggardly pride if they enfranchised their slaves grudgingly, and that he urges obedience first on the score of justice and then from the hope of remuneration. Gill puts the same in a line: the master was not to grudge the man his liberty, nor what he gives him when he dismisses him.
19:
Whose firstlings the prohibition covers is genuinely disputed. Henry takes the ban on working and shearing to concern the FEMALE firstlings, citing bishop Patrick, and reasons that though the females were not so entirely sanctified as the males, nor so early as at eight days old, they were still not to be converted by the owners to their own use; Wesley follows him and adds that even these must be offered as peace offerings or used in a religious feast. Keil and Calvin make no such distinction and read the ban of the firstborn generally, Keil spelling out the prohibited uses as yoking to plough or waggon and shearing. Calvin supplies the motive: a man might have used the ox's labour in ploughing, and might have sheared the lambs and then brought a deteriorated animal to the tabernacle, so God commands that what was due to him be honestly and absolutely paid.

Calvin then generalises, and the generalisation is his sharpest in the chapter. If good laws spring from evil habits, he says, it appears from this one with what audacious greediness men have always been led into wicked gains, since they had to be prohibited by express edict from enriching themselves at God's expense — and it is no wonder men are acute and sagacious in cheating one another, when they do not hesitate to deceive God by wicked artifices. Henry looks backwards instead, grounding the law in thankfulness for the sparing of Israel's firstborn when the firstborn of Egypt, of man and beast alike, were slain.

Who was to eat the firstling is the difficulty of the passage, and Ellicott states it squarely: this precept must somehow be squared with the law assigning the firstlings to the priests along with the first tithe, and the practical solution is to be sought in the practice of the Jews. He canvasses three answers. The Jewish commentator makes thou shalt eat refer to the priest. A second holds that the unblemished firstlings went to the priest and those unfit for sacrifice to the owner's household. Ellicott's own, which he thinks likeliest, is chronological: firstlings were collected at one time of year for the first tithe and given to the priests, and by the second tithe's collection there would generally be others born since, disposed of as these verses direct. Gill raises the same problem and offers two of the same solutions: if male firstlings are meant only priests might eat them, as Jarchi says, but if Israelites in general are addressed then female or second firstlings must be intended, voluntarily separated.

Ellicott also disposes of an apparent contradiction that nobody else notices, between the command here to sanctify the firstlings and the statement elsewhere that no man shall sanctify one. To sanctify here, he says, means to recognise them as Jehovah's property by not using them for ordinary purposes; the other passage forbids making a firstling the subject of a special vow, for the sufficient reason that it already belongs to him — and he argues this is the only reading consistent with a context dealing throughout with voluntary offerings.

The remaining provisions draw brief notes. Clarke observes of the eating at the chosen place that God in mercy made their duty and their interest go hand in hand, as he does with all his creatures — well, then, might Satan ask whether Job served God for naught, since he did not, and God designs that no man should. On the blemished animal Clarke is epigrammatic, that God will have both a perfect priest and a perfect offering; Gill explains the concession, that though it might not be sacrificed nor eaten as a feast at the sanctuary, it might be common food at home. Wesley glosses the yearly eating as taking place at the solemn feasts that returned annually, and Gill closes on the blood, poured upon the ground as water.
